Real-time Surgical View

Live video and vital signs, tested in the operating room

Live endoscopic video

We focused on reducing streaming delay so that viewing in XR could keep pace with the surgical monitor. With the CV-190, transmission reached Full HD per eye at around 60 fps.

Full HD streaming results↗

Video and vital signs together

In the STORZ operating room, we displayed endoscopic video alongside vital signs and checked waveform continuity against the bedside monitor.

How we connected the monitors↗

What comes next

Two directions build on the current Mac and XR apps.

Next development
Dedicated streaming hardware

XR Streaming Appliance

First, we’ll simplify input selection, streaming and reconnection in the Mac app. We’ll then explore moving capture, encoding and transmission into a dedicated device to reduce setup and operation in the operating room.

Research direction
Video and voice prototype

Multimodal Surgical Guidance

We’re exploring assistance that draws on surgical video and voice. The first step is to choose one task and the data it needs, then prototype what information to show in XR and when.

Intended Use & Regulatory Review

Defining intended use and reviewing medical device requirements

We’ll define the intended use of video display and transmission through the headset separately from AI assistance. As the scope takes shape, we’ll review whether each function falls within medical device regulation and what evaluation it needs.

Evaluation as development progresses

Measuring monitor-to-XR differences

We’ll record the monitor and XR display together using the same input, then measure delay, interruptions and recovery time. The same setup will let us compare future streaming hardware.

Viewing and interaction in the headset

We’ll compare screen layouts and controls using the same task, recording completion time, errors and visual comfort.
